extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; scientists interested in paradigm change and the nature of scientific discovery
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the criteria, signs, and processes Thomas Kuhn identifies as characteristic of scientific discovery, theory-induced findings, crisis, and the emergence of new theories (paradigm change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-induced discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculative or tentative (non-paradigm) theories can point the way to discovery; the discovery emerges only when experiment and tentative theory are articulated to a match.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though the term may seem paradoxical, during pre-paradigm periods and crises scientists generate many speculative, unarticulated theories that suggest experiments. Often the experimental result differs from the initial anticipation; only as experimental work and the tentative theory are jointly articulated does the discovery emerge and the theory become a paradigm. (Example: the Leyden jar’s emergence as experiments and theory were adjusted to fit.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior awareness of anomaly
rubrics_metrics.description: Discoveries that produce new kinds of phenomena commonly arise against a background of previously noticed anomalies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn repeatedly emphasizes that awareness of anomaly is a precursor: researchers notice something that doesn't fit existing expectations, which opens a period of investigation and conceptual adjustment leading to discovery. (Examples: anomalies leading to Leyden jar, chemical discoveries, astronomical discrepancies.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual and simultaneous observational and conceptual recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of a new phenomenon involves a gradual, often simultaneous, emergence of both observation (empirical detection) and conceptual reclassification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel phenomena are not immediately categorized correctly; observation and conceptual frameworks co-evolve until the anomaly becomes anticipated and the discovery is complete. The Bruner & Postman card experiment is used as a psychological analogue: anomalous stimuli are initially fit into existing categories and only with increased exposure do subjects adjust categories and recognize the anomaly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of paradigm categories and procedures (often with resistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Completion of a discovery typically requires changing the paradigm’s categories and procedures, a process often met by resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradigm change entails discarding some standard beliefs/procedures and replacing them with others; resistance is common and may accompany—and even serve a function in—this transition (e.g., ensuring anomalies penetrate to the core before abandonment of a paradigm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science prepares and constrains novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal scientific practice (specialized equipment, refined concepts, esoteric vocabulary and skills) both enables discovery and narrows vision, producing resistance to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professionalization leads to greater precision and sensitivity to anomaly (because instruments and expectations make deviations detectable) while also restricting scientists’ vision and causing reluctance to abandon established paradigms. The very apparatus and skills developed for anticipated functions make possible the observations that reveal novelty; yet the same professionalization fosters resistance that prevents premature surrender of the paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis as prerequisite for acceptable theory change
rubrics_metrics.description: A pronounced, prolonged awareness of anomaly (crisis) is generally required before large-scale, acceptable changes of theory are adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Copernican astronomy, Lavoisier’s chemistry, relativity) show that new major theories typically arise after the persistent failure of puzzles of normal science. Crisis involves failures that penetrate deeply and often last long enough to make the need for retooling apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symptoms/signs of crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain observable features indicate a field is in crisis: proliferation of competing versions of a theory, increasing vagueness and decreasing utility of the accepted theory, and breakdown of normal puzzle-solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn notes proliferation of alternative articulations (many versions of phlogiston theory), increasing complexity without improved accuracy (astronomy’s compounded circles), and repeated failures of existing rules as typical crisis signals. These symptoms typically appear a decade or two before a successful new theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proliferation of alternate theories during crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis commonly produces many competing theoretical constructions, reflecting the breakdown of the previous paradigm’s authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During crisis, scientists invent multiple alternatives to account for anomalies; such proliferation indicates that the paradigm no longer uniquely orders phenomena (example: multiple phlogiston variants; many ether-drag articulations before relativity).

rubrics_metrics.name: External/social factors modulate timing and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-technical (social, institutional, practical) pressures can affect when and how a breakdown is recognized and when paradigm change occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External pressures (e.g., need for calendar reform) may accelerate recognition of anomalies or direct attention to particular problems, but the core causal role in paradigm change is the technical breakdown within the science itself. Kuhn treats these external factors as significant for timing and recognition, though not the principal mechanism discussed in the essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous independent emergence as an index of preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: The frequent near-simultaneous emergence of the same scientific novelty from several laboratories indicates the thoroughness with which normal science prepared for that change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple independent confirmations show that normal science, though conservative, creates the conditions (precision, apparatus, problem focus) that allow the same anomaly to be detected and solved in different places, signalling both the traditional nature of normal science and the completeness of preparation for change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retooling is reserved for crisis (retooling as extravagance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists rarely invent radically new theoretical constructions except during pre-paradigm stages or crises; retooling scientific theory and practice is an ‘extravagance’ undertaken only when crisis indicates it is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As long as a paradigm’s tools solve defined problems, science moves fastest by confident use of those tools. The significance of crisis is that it signals the occasion when retooling (new methods, concepts, theories) is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and partial anticipation of novel theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel theories are often partially anticipated before crisis, but those anticipations are typically ignored in the absence of crisis because they do not address recognized failings of normal practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Aristarchus’ heliocentric idea or earlier anticipations of oxygen/combustion theories: without a recognized technical crisis, anticipatory ideas receive little attention. When persistent anomalies accumulate, earlier ignored anticipations may become relevant and be integrated into the new paradigm.
